title: Your short video is asking for attention before it gives anyone a reason to stay
markdown:
# Your short video is asking for attention before it gives anyone a reason to stay

At 8:47 p.m., the edit is finally done. The subtitles are clean, the lighting held up, and the useful part begins around second six. You post it anyway, then open the retention graph the next morning and see the familiar cliff near the start.

That cliff does not prove the whole video was bad. It says the opening made a stranger work too hard before offering a reason to stop scrolling.

If your videos regularly lose people in the first three seconds, this is the part to fix first. You do not need a louder personality or a fake promise. You need an opening that tells the right viewer what they will get if they stay.

## Start with the interruption you are earning

A scroll is a series of tiny decisions. The viewer is not judging your expertise yet. They are deciding whether this clip belongs to them.

"Hey, I wanted to talk about meal prep" may be friendly, but it makes the viewer wait for the point. So does "Three editing tips". Both name a subject. Neither creates much pressure to hear the next sentence.

Try opening with a problem that has already happened to the viewer:

"Your meal prep keeps tasting like leftovers because you pack it while it is still hot."

That line works because it narrows the audience and gives the next few seconds a job. A person whose lunches turn soggy has a reason to listen. Someone who does not care can keep moving, which is fine. A hook is allowed to exclude people.

The opening should make a promise your footage can keep. If the clip only shows one packing change, promise one packing change. Do not promise "the secret to meal prep" and then spend 25 seconds on a container lid.

## Give one idea five different beginnings

The first hook you write is usually a description of the video. It is rarely the best invitation into it. Before filming, make five openings that approach the same useful point from different directions.

For a video about keeping meal prep from getting watery, that could look like this:

- "Stop sealing your meal prep while the food is still steaming."
- "Why does your chicken turn watery by Wednesday?"
- "I changed one cooling step and stopped ruining lunch by day three."
- "If your meal prep tastes fine on Sunday and sad on Tuesday, watch this."
- "The lid is not the problem. The timing is."

These are not interchangeable. The first is direct and practical. The question works when the answer can arrive quickly. The personal version needs a real before-and-after you can show. The last one creates a small disagreement, so it needs a fast explanation.

Read each option aloud. If it takes two breaths, cut it. If the viewer must know your backstory to understand it, cut it. If the opening could sit on any creator's video, make it more specific to the problem you solve.

## Put proof beside the promise

Many hooks fail after they succeed. They make a sharp claim, then the video wanders into an introduction, a montage, or a long explanation. A viewer who stopped for an answer notices that delay.

Write the first ten seconds as one unit:

1. Say the hook.
2. Show the proof, result, or mistake named in the hook.
3. Explain the one thing the viewer should notice.

For the meal-prep example, the opening shot could show condensation trapped under a lid. Then show the same food cooling uncovered for a few minutes. The explanation can be simple: sealing hot food traps steam, and that moisture has somewhere to go.

That sequence gives the words something to lean on. It also helps you avoid borrowing a hook that does not fit your material. A financial creator may be able to open on a deadline. A baker may be able to open on a split cake. Use the tension you can actually put on screen.

## Test a variable, not your confidence

When a post underperforms, the temptation is to reshoot everything or decide that the platform buried it. Neither response tells you much.

Keep the topic and footage as steady as you can. Then test one change: a question instead of a warning, a closer opening shot, a different first line of on-screen text. Compare versions aimed at the same viewer. Look for the moment people leave, not just the final view count.

You are collecting evidence about your own audience. A cooking audience may stay for a visible mistake. A design audience may respond to a before-and-after. A service business may get attention when it names an expensive misunderstanding. There is no universal magic phrase, and that is useful news. It means you can stop chasing somebody else's formula.

## Use a first pass when the blank page is the bottleneck

This process takes a few minutes, which is exactly why it gets skipped when you are trying to post consistently. The result is a pile of videos that begin with the same soft introduction, even when the idea underneath is good.
